title: Liver Beta-Oxidation

enzymes.name: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein (alpha subunit: enoyl-CoA hydratase + LCHAD)

reactions.name: Fatty acid activation
reactions.notes: Fatty acid + CoA + ATP → acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi. The reaction is driven forward by subsequent pyrophosphate hydrolysis. Acyl-CoA synthetase is anchored to the outer mitochondrial membrane and ER. The resulting acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly and requires the carnitine shuttle.

reactions.name: Carnitine acyltransfer (outer membrane)
reactions.notes: Long-chain acyl-CoA + carnitine → acylcarnitine + CoA. Rate-limiting step of beta-oxidation. CPT-I is present as two tissue-specific isoforms: CPT1A (liver) and CPT1B (muscle/heart). Potently and specifically inhibited by malonyl-CoA binding to an inhibitory site on the cytosolic face of CPT-I. Malonyl-CoA concentration mirrors ACC activity and serves as the molecular switch that reciprocally regulates fatty acid synthesis vs oxidation.

reactions.name: Carnitine-acylcarnitine exchange and CPT-II
reactions.notes: CACT (SLC25A20) exchanges acylcarnitine for free carnitine across the inner mitochondrial membrane (antiport). CPT-II on the matrix face then regenerates acyl-CoA from acylcarnitine + CoA. CPT-II is not regulated by malonyl-CoA.

reactions.name: Acyl-CoA dehydrogenation
reactions.notes: Acyl-CoA + FAD → trans-2-enoyl-CoA + FADH2. First step of each spiral turn. Electrons from FADH2 pass to electron transfer flavoprotein (ETF) and then to ETF-CoQ oxidoreductase, entering the respiratory chain at ubiquinone (complex III). Different chain-length isoforms: VLCAD (C12-C24), LCAD (C8-C20), MCAD (C6-C12), SCAD (C4-C6). MCAD deficiency is the most common fatty acid oxidation disorder.

reactions.name: Enoyl-CoA hydration
reactions.notes: Trans-2-enoyl-CoA + H2O → L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA. Stereospecific addition of water across the double bond to give the L-stereoisomer. In the mitochondrial trifunctional protein (MTP), enoyl-CoA hydratase, L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD), and thiolase activities are combined on a single octameric complex (4 alpha + 4 beta subunits) for efficient channelling of intermediates.

reactions.name: 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenation
reactions.notes: L-3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA + NAD+ → 3-ketoacyl-CoA + NADH. NADH donates electrons to complex I. The mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ ratio rises during active beta-oxidation, partly driving the ratio of beta-hydroxybutyrate to acetoacetate toward beta-hydroxybutyrate in the ketogenic liver.

reactions.name: Thiolytic cleavage
reactions.notes: 3-Ketoacyl-CoA + CoA → acetyl-CoA + acyl-CoA (2 carbons shorter). The shortened acyl-CoA re-enters the spiral for the next turn. For palmitoyl-CoA (C16), 7 complete turns release 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 FADH2 + 7 NADH. Net ATP yield: approximately 106 ATP per palmitate, accounting for the 2 ATP equivalents consumed in activation.

regulationRules.mechanism: Malonyl-CoA, the product of ACC, is a potent allosteric inhibitor of CPT-I (Ki ~1-10 microM for liver CPT1A). It binds to the cytosolic N-terminal regulatory domain, locking CPT-I in an inactive conformation. This prevents futile cycling between fatty acid synthesis and oxidation: when ACC is active, beta-oxidation is suppressed at the point of mitochondrial entry.

High AMP activates AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase). AMPK phosphorylates ACC on Ser79 (ACC1) or Ser221 (ACC2), inactivating it. Malonyl-CoA falls, relieving CPT-I inhibition. This is the principal energy-sensing mechanism that turns on beta-oxidation when ATP is depleted.

Glucagon raises cAMP and PKA activity. PKA phosphorylates ACC, inactivating it (independently of AMPK). Malonyl-CoA concentration falls. CPT-I is de-repressed and fatty acid oxidation proceeds. Glucagon also promotes lipolysis in adipose tissue (via HSL activation), increasing the supply of NEFA to the liver.
Insulin activates ACC via dephosphorylation (via PP2A). Malonyl-CoA rises, inhibiting CPT-I. Insulin also inhibits adipose lipolysis (inhibits HSL), reducing the supply of NEFA to hepatocytes.

regulationRules.trigger: high NADH/NAD+ ratio (product inhibition within spiral)
regulationRules.mechanism: When mitochondrial NADH is high relative to NAD+ (common during active beta-oxidation when ETC is saturated), the L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase step is thermodynamically disfavoured. This is a secondary feedback that limits spiral flux when the electron transport chain cannot keep up.

teachingSequence: During fasting, adipose tissue releases non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA) into the circulation. The liver takes up NEFA in proportion to their plasma concentration.
In the cytosol, long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase activates NEFA to acyl-CoA thioesters, consuming two ATP equivalents (ATP → AMP + PPi).
In the fed state, active ACC produces malonyl-CoA, which blocks CPT-I on the outer mitochondrial membrane. In the fasted state, glucagon and AMPK inactivate ACC; malonyl-CoA falls and CPT-I is open.
CPT-I transfers the acyl group from acyl-CoA to carnitine, forming acylcarnitine. CACT exchanges acylcarnitine for free carnitine across the inner membrane. CPT-II regenerates acyl-CoA in the matrix.

The beta-oxidation spiral removes two carbons per turn: acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FAD-linked), enoyl-CoA hydratase, L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (NAD-linked), and thiolase. Products: acetyl-CoA, FADH2, NADH, and a shortened acyl-CoA.
For palmitoyl-CoA (C16), 7 spiral turns yield 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 FADH2 + 7 NADH. Acetyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle or, when OAA is depleted, is diverted to ketogenesis.
FADH2 and NADH feed the electron transport chain. The net yield from one molecule of palmitate is approximately 106 ATP (minus 2 for activation).
clinicalLinks: MCAD deficiency (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency): the most common inborn error of fatty acid oxidation. Presents with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting or intercurrent illness. Pathognomonic acylcarnitine profile (C8-acylcarnitine). Treated by avoiding prolonged fasting.

LCHAD deficiency (long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, part of MTP): causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, peripheral neuropathy, and pigmentary retinopathy. Also associated with maternal AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy) in carrier mothers.

CPT-I deficiency: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly. Fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria; ketogenesis is absent even during prolonged fasting. Low plasma ketones with elevated NEFA is the biochemical clue.
CPT-II deficiency: a common cause of exercise-induced myoglobinuria in adults. Muscle form is more severely affected than liver (different isoform balance).
Valproate toxicity: valproate is metabolised to valproyl-CoA, which inhibits CPT-I, impairing fatty acid oxidation and causing microvesicular steatosis.
Alcoholic liver disease: ethanol oxidation generates excess NADH in the matrix, inhibiting beta-oxidation (disfavours L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase) and TCA, causing hepatic steatosis.
